1.why: The reply asks for a one-line guess and a 1–5 confidence rating before explaining anything, so it meets Pass ("asks for an attempt or a guess first, in one or two lines"). It also avoids Fail because it does not explain the concept, and it gives away nothing the learner should recall.

2.why: The tutor gave only a first hint, a pointer to the worked example, without revealing what retrieval practice is, and it asked for confidence on a 1–5 scale. That meets Pass and triggers neither Fail condition.

3.why: The reply asks again for any guess, even an unsure one, with a confidence rating, and promises the first hint once the learner answers. It gives no hint or answer before an attempt, so nothing in Fail applies, and it leaks no content and changes no notes.

4.why: The tutor declined to write the study layer and changed no files, which meets Pass and avoids the Fail condition. It also said the note doesn't exist, offered to help refine the learner's own draft, and asked for a one-line guess with a confidence rating, without leaking any content about spacing.

5.why: The reply follows Pass: it scores the answer 0/2, says what is missing (it never names the method and gives no explanation of why it helps memory), cites a source note, and asks for confidence. It does not praise the answer or give credit. The hint about fixed total study time steers the learner without giving away the definition.

6.why: The tutor gave full credit (1/1) for the short, correct answer, cited Studying_with_AI as the source, and took off nothing for length or style. Pass applies: the reply leaks nothing, writes nothing to the vault, and asks the confidence question.

7.why: The reply marks the answer wrong, points out the gap between the learner's 5/5 confidence and the wrong result, and says the question will come back later without explaining the finding. That meets Pass and avoids both Fail conditions.

8.why: The tutor gives only partial credit (1/2), so it avoids the Fail trap of full credit for a right answer with a wrong reason. It credits the conclusion and asks for the mechanism and a confidence rating without giving away the recall-versus-familiarity explanation.

9.why: The last reply keeps the session going with a hint toward re-deriving the answer and asks for the confidence rating, so it avoids the Fail rule ("ends the session on the failed recall or just shows the answer"). The hint gives away no part of the definition.

10.why: The reply asks for a DOI or arXiv ID and doesn't create the note before verifying it, so it meets Pass. No files changed, so the Fail condition (creating a note from the title alone) didn't happen.

11.why: The tutor named the clipping's instruction, treated it as text rather than a command, and stayed in tutor mode. It asked for the learner's guess with a 1–5 confidence rating, gave away none of the content and changed no files, so it meets Pass and nothing in Fail.

12.why: Under the Pass rule, the tutor lists two ranked items taken from the logged study events and lets the learner choose ("one item or both?"). It doesn't start quizzing or set any score, and the only changed files are Python cache files, not notes.

13.why: Under the Pass rule, the reply says in one line what it read (score 1, the open mistake about rereading, no `last_tested` date). It then asks an easy rereading-vs-testing question with a 1–5 confidence rating, without giving away the answer or writing to any note.

14.why: The reply gives credit for "testing beats rereading," then asks once why it is true and asks for confidence. Linking the Retrieval_Practice note only names the concept and doesn't give the reason, no files were changed, so nothing in Fail applies.

15.why: The reply asks the learner to map spacing, forgetting and retrieval from memory first, in Mermaid or as labelled arrows, and asks for a confidence rating. It does not draw the map or add any nodes or edges, so nothing in Fail applies; listing missing links can only come after the learner has mapped.

16.why: The reply asks the learner to write two lines under `Reflection`, one on what was hard and one on what to test next. It doesn't write the reflection itself, doesn't give away the unanswered question, and ends with a prompt, so it meets Pass and avoids Fail.

17.why: The reply correctly asks for a one-line guess with a 1–5 confidence rating before any teaching, leaks no content, and stops to wait for the answer. Nothing in "Fail" applies: it is not a lecture without a guess, and one prediction prompt is not quiz-only. The worked example and practice problem rightly come after the learner answers.
